stories.title: Cligès (Chrétien de Troyes)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Cliges uses courtly intrigue and an apparent-death strategy to negotiate love and dynastic barriers within a romance conscious of other lovers' stories.
stories.analysis: Cliges uses courtly intrigue and an apparent-death strategy to negotiate love and dynastic barriers within a romance conscious of other lovers' stories.
stories.instruction: Let characters knowingly seek an alternative to a famous tragic pattern, but make their workaround create concrete ethical and practical risks.

stories.title: Parzival (Wolfram von Eschenbach)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Parzival's development connects martial identity with the capacity to respond to another person's suffering rather than merely perform correct manners.
stories.analysis: Parzival's development connects martial identity with the capacity to respond to another person's suffering rather than merely perform correct manners.
stories.instruction: Make growth culminate in a question or action attending to someone else's need, supported by earlier failures of perception.

stories.title: Tristan and Iseult (Gottfried von Strassburg / Thomas of Britain)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.attribution: Gottfried von Strassburg / Thomas of Britain; distinct textual traditions
stories.teaser: The lovers' attachment conflicts with marriage, kingship, and loyalty; potion traditions complicate the relation between choice and compulsion.
stories.analysis: The lovers' attachment conflicts with marriage, kingship, and loyalty; potion traditions complicate the relation between choice and compulsion.
stories.instruction: Specify how much agency a binding force removes, then explore the choices that remain instead of using enchantment to excuse every consequence.

stories.title: The Alliterative Morte Arthure
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: The Alliterative Morte Arthure emphasizes Arthur's imperial warfare before betrayal and collapse, giving expansion a distinct place in the tragedy.
stories.analysis: The Alliterative Morte Arthure emphasizes Arthur's imperial warfare before betrayal and collapse, giving expansion a distinct place in the tragedy.
stories.instruction: Make external success draw resources away from internal stability, and trace how an absent ruler's campaign creates a domestic opening.

stories.title: The Stanzaic Morte Arthur
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: The Stanzaic Morte Arthur foregrounds the Lancelot-Guinevere crisis and its consequences for fellowship and succession.
stories.analysis: The Stanzaic Morte Arthur foregrounds the Lancelot-Guinevere crisis and its consequences for fellowship and succession.
stories.instruction: Let a private breach become public through a specific accuser or event, then show why institutional loyalties prevent an easy settlement.

stories.title: The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Gawain's response to Ragnelle's question gives her sovereignty over an intimate choice, making the resolution depend on relinquishing control.
stories.analysis: Gawain's response to Ragnelle's question gives her sovereignty over an intimate choice, making the resolution depend on relinquishing control.
stories.instruction: Give the apparent helper a withheld choice of their own, and let respecting it resolve a conflict force or bargaining cannot.

stories.title: The High History of the Holy Grail (Perlesvaus)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Perlesvaus develops a severe, episodic Grail world in which spiritual authority and violence are tightly entangled.
stories.analysis: Perlesvaus develops a severe, episodic Grail world in which spiritual authority and violence are tightly entangled.
stories.instruction: Give a sacred quest competing interpretations of rightful action, and avoid assuming that the protagonist's religious claim automatically validates violence.
notes: The source's spiritual justification of violence is a subject of interpretation, not automatically endorsed guidance.

stories.title: Beowulf (Anonymous Old English Epic)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Beowulf's early monster victories and final dragon fight compare personal prowess with a king's responsibility for a vulnerable future.
stories.analysis: Beowulf's early monster victories and final dragon fight compare personal prowess with a king's responsibility for a vulnerable future.
stories.instruction: Repeat a similar heroic challenge at a later life stage, changing who depends on the protagonist and what their death would leave unresolved.

stories.title: The Nibelungenlied (Middle High German Epic)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Siegfried's murder and Kriemhild's later revenge turn familial and political loyalties into an expanding catastrophe.
stories.analysis: Siegfried's murder and Kriemhild's later revenge turn familial and political loyalties into an expanding catastrophe.
stories.instruction: Carry a concealed injury across a time jump, showing how new power changes the injured person's capacity and willingness to retaliate.

stories.title: The Song of Roland (La Chanson de Roland)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Roland's delay in calling for aid makes personal honor consequential for the rearguard's survival.
stories.analysis: Roland's delay in calling for aid makes personal honor consequential for the rearguard's survival.
stories.instruction: Give a protagonist a timely means of requesting help, then make a status belief delay its use until the cost becomes irreversible.

stories.title: The Poem of the Cid (Cantar de Mio Cid)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: The Cid rebuilds standing through campaigns and alliances, while his daughters' mistreatment requires a public process of redress.
stories.analysis: The Cid rebuilds standing through campaigns and alliances, while his daughters' mistreatment requires a public process of redress.
stories.instruction: Separate recovering status from repairing harm, and give vulnerable family members claims that military success alone cannot settle.

stories.title: Piers Plowman (William Langland)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Langland's dream visions turn the search for truthful living into encounters with social roles, competing teachings, and unstable interpretations.
stories.analysis: Langland's dream visions turn the search for truthful living into encounters with social roles, competing teachings, and unstable interpretations.
stories.instruction: Personify a contested value through several figures with incompatible practices, then anchor the debate in concrete work and obligations.

stories.title: The Canterbury Tales (Geoffrey Chaucer)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Pilgrims tell stories within a social contest, allowing teller identity, interruption, and response to change a tale's meaning.
stories.analysis: Pilgrims tell stories within a social contest, allowing teller identity, interruption, and response to change a tale's meaning.
stories.instruction: Give each narrator a stake in how listeners judge the story, and let the next tale answer a tension created by the previous telling.
notes: All 24 conventional tale slots plus the General Prologue are represented; unfinished tales and non-narrative prose retain their actual forms.
Conventional 24 tale slots and General Prologue covered; internal prologue and subepisode analysis is selective.

children.title: The Knight's Tale
children.analysis: Two imprisoned cousins' rivalry becomes a public tournament whose result still fails to deliver simple control over love and fortune.
children.instruction: Let an authority design rules to contain conflict, then distinguish winning the procedure from achieving the desired life.

children.title: The Miller's Tale
children.analysis: A fabricated catastrophe creates room for an affair, while another suitor's intervention makes the deceptions collide physically.
children.instruction: Give each deceiver an independent objective and incomplete information, then stage a collision caused by their conflicting plans.

children.title: The Reeve's Tale
children.analysis: Students' response to a dishonest miller entangles theft, sexual conduct, and a disruptive household night.
children.instruction: Make retaliation exploit the wrongdoer's ordinary system, while examining the collateral harm and unequal power within the joke.

children.title: The Cook's Tale
children.analysis: The surviving fragment introduces an apprentice's dissipated conduct without supplying a completed moral or plot resolution.
children.instruction: Use a few specific work habits to establish a character, and label any supplied ending as original continuation rather than Chaucer's text.

children.title: The Man of Law's Tale
children.analysis: Custance's repeated displacement and false accusations make identity persist across changing political and domestic settings.
children.instruction: Let an exiled character carry one consistent commitment through different institutions, varying how each setting rewards or endangers it.

children.title: The Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale
children.analysis: The teller's self-authorizing prologue frames a tale whose central question concerns women's wishes and sovereignty within marriage.
children.instruction: Give a narrator a personal stake in the lesson, and make the plot test who gets to choose rather than simply repeat the narrator's claim.

children.title: The Friar's Tale
children.analysis: A summoner's dealings with a disguised devil expose exploitative collection and the difference between formulaic curses and actual intention.
children.instruction: Make an antagonist misuse an official role, and give judgment a specific criterion that the antagonist initially misunderstands.

children.title: The Summoner's Tale
children.analysis: A friar's demand for a gift produces a bodily joke and an elaborate problem of dividing it equally.
children.instruction: Turn an exploitative demand into a literal distribution problem that reveals the demander's assumptions about entitlement.

children.title: The Clerk's Tale
children.analysis: Walter's tests subject Griselda to cruelty, making endurance inseparable from questions about the tester's authority.
children.instruction: If using a loyalty test, center the tested person's losses and distinguish patience from approval of the conditions imposed.

children.title: The Merchant's Tale
children.analysis: January's confidence and blindness interact with May's affair, while supernatural intervention makes seeing insufficient to settle interpretation.
children.instruction: Give a character strong reasons to prefer an explanation, and show how direct evidence can be rhetorically reinterpreted.

children.title: The Squire's Tale
children.analysis: Marvellous gifts and a speaking falcon open several narrative possibilities that the surviving telling does not complete.
children.instruction: Introduce wonders through distinct functions, then choose and label an original causal spine instead of claiming the source resolves every thread.

children.title: The Franklin's Tale
children.analysis: An impossible-looking condition becomes apparently fulfilled, forcing several people to decide whether to enforce claims or release others from them.
children.instruction: Build a chain of enforceable obligations, then let each participant's voluntary release change what the next person can choose.

children.title: The Physician's Tale
children.analysis: A corrupt authority's attempt to seize Virginia culminates in her father's lethal response, making institutional and familial protection deeply troubling.
children.instruction: Do not treat a protector's violence as inevitable; show alternative choices and give the threatened person a perspective on the claimed protection.

children.title: The Pardoner's Prologue and Tale
children.analysis: A speaker admits exploiting an anti-greed message, then tells of seekers whose found treasure turns them against one another.
children.instruction: Let a narrator articulate a valid warning while violating it, and keep the story's insight distinct from the narrator's integrity.

children.title: The Shipman's Tale
children.analysis: A loan, an affair, and a repayment claim let the same money acquire different meanings across a household triangle.
children.instruction: Track one resource through several exchanges, ensuring each participant's account is locally plausible but incompatible with another's.

children.title: The Prioress's Tale
children.analysis: A devotional miracle is built around an antisemitic accusation, requiring separation of narrative technique from the harmful claim it promotes.
children.instruction: Study restricted viewpoint and miraculous testimony without reproducing a marginalized community as a stock villain or treating the accusation as history.

children.title: Sir Thopas
children.analysis: The deliberately conventional romance performance is interrupted, making the audience's refusal part of the joke.
children.instruction: Exaggerate recognizable genre formulas, then give an in-world listener a concrete reason to challenge the performance.

children.title: The Tale of Melibee
children.analysis: After violence against his household, Melibee's decision is shaped through extended counsel, particularly Prudence's arguments against hasty retaliation.
children.instruction: Give revenge a genuine deliberative phase with competing advisers, each addressing a concrete likely consequence.

children.title: The Monk's Tale
children.analysis: A sequence of prominent figures' reversals tests the force and limits of repeatedly explaining downfall through fortune.
children.instruction: Use brief parallel examples to build a pattern, then include a contrasting case that prompts the listener to question its simplicity.

children.title: The Nun's Priest's Tale
children.analysis: A fox catches Chanticleer through flattering speech, but speaking again allows a reversal of the trap.
children.instruction: Make the same communicative weakness expose both victim and deceiver at different moments.

children.title: The Second Nun's Tale
children.analysis: Cecilia's life and martyrdom present steadfast religious witness against coercive authority within a saint's-life form.
children.instruction: Give a resisting character a specific demand they refuse and a community affected by that refusal; identify the narrator's devotional framing.

children.title: The Canon's Yeoman's Tale
children.analysis: An assistant's account exposes the costs and manipulations behind alchemical promises, connecting technical opacity to exploitation.
children.instruction: Let an insider reveal the labor, materials, and staged proof behind a supposed breakthrough, rather than debunking it through assertion alone.

children.title: The Manciple's Tale
children.analysis: A truth-telling crow suffers for revealing betrayal, making accurate speech dangerous within unequal emotional power.
children.instruction: Give a messenger true information but limited protection, and make the listener's reaction expose what truth threatens.

children.title: The Parson's Tale
children.analysis: The final prose discourse shifts away from entertaining plots toward an organized account of repentance and conduct.
children.instruction: When ending an episodic work with reflection, tie its ethical categories to choices the audience has already seen rather than adding unrelated doctrine.

children.title: The General Prologue
children.analysis: Descriptions of the pilgrims establish tensions between professional ideals, personal conduct, and the narrator's judgments.
children.instruction: Introduce a group through details that reveal both role and contradiction, giving later stories a social context.

stories.title: Kudrun (Middle High German Epic)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Kudrun's captivity and eventual settlement contrast suffering and martial rescue with possibilities for reconciliation across hostile families.
stories.analysis: Kudrun's captivity and eventual settlement contrast suffering and martial rescue with possibilities for reconciliation across hostile families.
stories.instruction: Give a captive sustained choices within limited power, then make the final settlement address future relations rather than only punish former enemies.

stories.title: Waldere (Old English Fragment)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: The surviving Waldere fragments preserve exhortation and weapon-centered heroic conflict without a complete extant plot.
stories.analysis: The surviving Waldere fragments preserve exhortation and weapon-centered heroic conflict without a complete extant plot.
stories.instruction: Use a decisive speech to reveal obligations and fear, but label any reconstructed surrounding action as original adaptation rather than source fact.
notes: Only fragments survive; the surrounding complete plot is not asserted.

stories.title: The Battle of Maldon (Old English Poem)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Byrhtnoth's decision at the crossing precedes defeat, after which retainers' responses expose differing meanings of loyalty; ofermod remains interpretively contested.
stories.analysis: Byrhtnoth's decision at the crossing precedes defeat, after which retainers' responses expose differing meanings of loyalty; ofermod remains interpretively contested.
stories.instruction: Make a leader's tactical decision specific, then give followers distinct choices after its failure rather than treating loyalty as a single response.
notes: Meaning of ofermod and the poem's judgment of the leader are contested.

stories.title: Dream of the Rood (Old English Poem)
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: The cross speaks as a witness and participant, recasting apparent defeat through a perspective that combines burden, obedience, and transformation.
stories.analysis: The cross speaks as a witness and participant, recasting apparent defeat through a perspective that combines burden, obedience, and transformation.
stories.instruction: Let an object narrate an event it materially endured, using its limited access and changed function to reframe familiar action.

stories.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (Washington Irving)

stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Ichabod's disappearance admits supernatural and socially motivated readings, with rivalry and local storytelling shaping what survives as explanation.
stories.analysis: Ichabod's disappearance admits supernatural and socially motivated readings, with rivalry and local storytelling shaping what survives as explanation.
stories.instruction: Plant evidence compatible with two accounts, and give the community a reason to prefer one without fully proving it.

stories.title: Rip Van Winkle (Washington Irving)
stories.tradition: Global Cryptids, Urban Folklore & Folk Hero Ballads
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: Rip's long absence makes familiar places politically and socially strange, separating bodily continuity from belonging to a changed community.
stories.analysis: Rip's long absence makes familiar places politically and socially strange, separating bodily continuity from belonging to a changed community.
stories.instruction: Send a character across a major social transition, and reveal change through ordinary names, routines, and relationships rather than a history lecture.

stories.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin (Robert Browning)
stories.tradition: Global Cryptids, Urban Folklore & Folk Hero Ballads
stories.section: Chivalric Romances, Heroic Cycles & Global Folklore
stories.teaser: A town accepts extraordinary service and then refuses compensation, turning a solved collective problem into a retaliatory loss.
stories.analysis: A town accepts extraordinary service and then refuses compensation, turning a solved collective problem into a retaliatory loss.
stories.instruction: Make the contract and service visible, give officials a specific excuse for refusal, and decide who bears a punishment they did not choose.

stories.title: The Flying Dutchman

notes: The Wagner child record is one named adaptation, not a universal version of the legend.

children.title: Wagner's Flying Dutchman: Senta's vow
children.analysis: Senta hears and retells the Dutchman's legend before identifying herself with its possible release, making an embedded story shape action.
children.instruction: Let a character adopt a role from a story they believe, then test whether they understand its real demands; retain the opera's identity as one adaptation.

stories.title: The Bell Witch Legend

children.title: The Bell household disturbances
children.analysis: The legend develops through reported noises, physical disturbances, and a speaking presence around a household, rather than independently verified supernatural evidence.
children.instruction: Escalate incidents through different witnesses and observable effects, keeping the narrator's certainty distinct from each participant's claim.

children.title: The Bell Witch's later public revival
children.analysis: The 1937 revival included a radio dramatization, showing how a local legend acquires a new performance frame and public audience.
children.instruction: When a legend is adapted into a new medium, make the changed audience and incentives part of the story's framing.

children.title: La Llorona in Hawes's juvenile-hall accounts
children.analysis: Hawes records young people's accounts connecting La Llorona to danger in institutions and foster settings; these are attributed narratives, not a universal origin.
children.instruction: Let a familiar warning change meaning inside an institution, and show who repeats it, who is frightened, and what behavior it regulates.

children.title: La Llorona in Janvier's Mexico City account
children.analysis: Janvier's published account presents the weeping figure through a local speaker's city-at-night knowledge.
children.instruction: Give a ghost story a speaker with a reason to warn a newcomer, using named places to make the advice actionable.

notes: Reported sightings are not treated as proof of a new species.

children.title: Puerto Rico's 1995 chupacabra reports
children.analysis: Reports connect livestock deaths with an unfamiliar creature description, giving a community's unexplained harm a circulating name.
children.instruction: Start with a tangible loss, then show how witnesses and media attach different interpretations before the evidence is settled.

children.title: The later canine chupacabra image
children.analysis: Later alleged specimens and sightings often involve diseased canids, illustrating a change in the creature's popular description rather than proof of one consistent animal.
children.instruction: Let investigators compare an emerging image with earlier testimony, separating explanation of one case from claims about every report.

stories.title: The Mothman Chronicles

children.title: The Point Pleasant sightings
children.analysis: Winged-creature reports centered near Point Pleasant's former munitions site in 1966, creating a geographically concentrated legend.
children.instruction: Use recurring location and sensory details to connect reports, while preserving differences between witnesses rather than forcing agreement.

children.title: Keel's Silver Bridge connection
children.analysis: Keel's later account connects strange reports with the 1967 bridge collapse; the connection is an interpretation, not an established cause.
children.instruction: Give characters information before and after a disaster, showing how knowledge of the outcome changes what they call a warning.

stories.title: The Jersey Devil Legend

stories.analysis: Jersey Devil traditions join a monstrous birth story to later sightings, with versions shaped by local conflict and family stigma.

notes: Expanded into selected independently useful narrative units; not an exhaustive chapter-by-chapter or regional-variant catalogue.

children.title: Mother Leeds' thirteenth child
children.analysis: The Pinelands Commission's retelling connects a parent's rejection of a thirteenth child to a monstrous transformation and departure.
children.instruction: Make an origin account reveal communal fears about family and belonging, without endorsing its stigmatizing explanation as factual history.

children.title: The Jersey Devil as a Pinelands protector
children.analysis: The Commission also notes a modern protective interpretation of a figure otherwise associated with frightening encounters.
children.instruction: Change a community's relationship to a feared being through a new shared threat, while preserving evidence of why earlier stories differed.

children.title: Blackwood's The Wendigo
children.analysis: In Blackwood's literary horror, Defago's disappearance and altered return unsettle the boundary between a recognizable companion and the surrounding wilderness.

children.title: Babe the Blue Ox in Brown's collection
children.analysis: Charles E. Brown's collected Bunyan material gives the giant logger an enormous blue ox whose strength magnifies ordinary lumbering labor.

children.analysis: Collected birth and infancy stories extend the adult logger's impossible size into his beginnings, making origin itself part of occupational comedy.

stories.title: Pecos Bill and the Cyclone
